title: Alef
hook: a silent letter; the rabbis note the Ten Words begin with it (anochi)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the line that starts on the right, and the word Shema traced leftward. Your line was right to left. What did you read slowly? Today, the first letter, on the far right of the alef-bet. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-nine.

A mountain wrapped in smoke. Thunder, lightning, the sound of a horn growing louder and louder. The people stand at the foot of Sinai, shaking. And then God speaks. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation, the first words are "I am the LORD thy God." In Hebrew, the very first word is anochi. I am. Look at how it's spelled, and there's a surprise. Anochi begins with alef, the first letter of the alphabet. And alef, on its own, makes no sound at all. All that thunder, and the first word opens on a silent letter. Today's word is that letter.
screen: `SMOKE, THUNDER, A HORN.` → `ANOCHI: I AM.` → `IT BEGINS WITH A SILENT LETTER.`

segments.voice: Alef. Turn it four ways. First, the sound that isn't there. Alef has no sound of its own. It holds a place. Whatever vowel is written with it, that's what you hear: ah, or eh, or oh. It's the open mouth before the word. Second, a midrash. The rabbis noticed that the Torah's first word, bereshit, in the beginning, starts with bet, the second letter. So an old midrash tells a story: alef comes before God and complains. I'm the first letter, and you began the world with bet? And God answers: wait. When I give the Torah at Sinai, I will begin with you. And the Ten Words do open with anochi, with alef. The silent letter was saved for the moment of revelation. Third, the later teachers. Some later Jewish teachers pushed the thought further. They asked what the people at Sinai could really bear to hear, and suggested that perhaps it was the alef alone: the silent opening, before any word, and that was enough. It's a teaching, not a claim about history, but it gives silence an honored place at the mountain. Fourth, an ordinary day. Everyday talk often rushes past the alef. We start speaking before we've finished listening. Alef sits at the head of the alphabet as a reminder that the open mouth, the breath before the word, comes first. In this alphabet, before bet and every letter after it, there is a letter you can see and cannot hear.
screen: `A LETTER WITH NO SOUND.` · `ALEF'S COMPLAINT, GOD'S PROMISE.` · `PERHAPS ONLY THE ALEF.` · `THE BREATH BEFORE THE WORD.` · then, large: `ALEF IS SILENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a minute of alef. Settle, and breathe. Let your mouth fall slightly open, the way it does just before a word. Don't say the word. Stay right there, at the opening. When a thought arrives, let it pass the way a sound passes in another room. Then come back to the open mouth and the breath moving through it. No words. Just the place where words begin. If you pray, you can let this silence be the doorway into your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Alef. The first letter: silent on its own, the open mouth before the word, and the start of anochi at Sinai. Today's word.
Your line: alef is silent. Today, in one conversation, take a single silent breath before you answer. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Jewish learners meet alef first, as a silent letter that carries its vowel; the rabbis teach that the Ten Commandments open with anochi, 'I am', which begins with alef.
